newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU played for time at grain tender, traders say.
newsitem.headline: EU played for time at grain tender, traders say.

text.p: The European Union slowed its wheat sales and also pared subsidies this week, but traders said this mostly unexpected move was not a policy change.

The dollar is holding most of its recent strength and export rivals Australia, Canada and Argentina have logistical hurdles, suggesting the EU has time to touch the brakes on refunds before committing to the next wave of exports.
"The ball is a little more in the EU's court on exports this week. At the same time they can afford to wait and put a bit more pressure on the domestic market," said one trade source.
The EU on Thursday awarded licences for 115,000 tonnes of soft wheat at a maximum refund of 17.99 Ecus per tonne, compared with 211,350 tonnes for one Ecu more the previous week.
Traders had been expecting a refund closer to 18.5 Ecus, which would have released exports of some 250,000 tonnes -- more in step with the EU's weekly average.

Another blamed the decision on firmer U.S. futures and a slightly higher dollar than a week before. U.S. wheat prices had to fall somewhat to compete again, and the country's crop was nearly sold out.
"So the trade was expecting 18.50, but it's not much of a difference," he said.
He and others saw little urgency in the regular tender this week.
"All the shorts are further forward," he said.
Licences needed on wheat for Egypt were all for April and March, while delays in shipments to Iraq meant there was no hurry for licences to do that business.
One trader said the EU's grain managers might also have been waiting for the next export news.
"They might have had a sniff of the Iran business," he said, referring to an Iranian purchase of an estimated 200,000 to 400,000 tonnes of French wheat that emerged on Friday morning.
But others argued the wheat award -- valued at $143 per tonne fob France for February and $1-2 less for March -- was in step with the world market and said there had been no surprises.
The move was definitely not a signal that the EU was going to hold the refund below 18.00 Ecus, one exporter said.
"After all, they've given 19.00 in the past," he added.
The EU is seen as unwilling for now to break below $140 per tonne as a world market equivalent for French wheat.
